intro: In August 1914 a soldier marched off to war with a rifle, a horse-drawn wagon behind him and a letter home that would take a week to arrive. His great-granddaughter carries in her pocket a device that can reach any person on Earth in a second, and she lives in a world with about eight billion people, nearly two hundred countries, and enough nuclear weapons to end civilization in an afternoon. Between those two lives lie two world wars that killed tens of millions, the rise and fall of dictatorships that claimed the right to control every thought, a forty-year standoff between two superpowers, the end of the European empires, and the wiring together of the whole planet. This unit covers that century.

The three chapters follow a shape. The first, from 1914 to 1945, shows how modern states learned to organize whole societies for war and, in the worst cases, for murder, and how the world tried twice to build something to stop it happening again. The second, from 1945 to 1991, follows a divided world in which the superpowers never fought each other directly but fought through Korea, Vietnam, Afghanistan and dozens of other places, while more than half of humanity, in India, Africa, Asia and the Middle East, won independence from empires. The third, from 1991 to today, is about the world those endings made: one connected economy, a rising China, wars that began on a single morning in 2001, and problems such as climate, disease, migration and inequality that no border can hold back.

You will read the evidence: a soldier's letter from a Christmas truce, a president's words after Pearl Harbor, the Nazis' own train schedules, a leader's statement from the dock at his trial, a curve of carbon dioxide measured on a Hawaiian volcano. You will meet people who held total power and people who stood in front of tanks, and you will see how the same event can carry two names for two peoples. By the end you should be able to explain how the twentieth century made the world you live in, to argue with evidence about who gained and who paid, and to bring a historian's habits to the flood of news that reaches your own screen every day.
bigQuestion: From 1914 to today, what did people learn, and fail to learn, about how much power a government should hold over its own people and over the world?

test.q: Why did a killing in Sarajevo in 1914 become a war among all the great powers within five weeks?
choices: Because Serbia invaded Germany
Because the alliance system pulled each power in as its partner was threatened, and war plans left no time to talk
Because the League of Nations ordered it
Because Britain wanted Austria's colonies
test.why: Germany backed Austria, Russia backed Serbia, France and Britain were tied to Russia, and mobilization plans made each step trigger the next.

test.q: What did the machine gun, artillery and barbed wire do to warfare on the Western Front?
choices: They made cavalry charges more effective
They ended the war within months
They made attacking across open ground so deadly that both sides dug trenches and the front barely moved for years
They were banned by both sides after 1915
test.why: Defense became far stronger than attack, so battles like the Somme cost enormous casualties for a few miles of ground.

test.q: Which promise won Lenin's Bolsheviks support among soldiers, peasants and workers in 1917?
choices: Victory over Germany
A restored tsar
Free elections within a year
Peace, land and bread
test.why: Each word spoke to a group the temporary government had failed: war-weary soldiers, land-hungry peasants and hungry city workers.

test.q: How did the Great Depression help bring Hitler to power?
choices: Mass unemployment after 1929 turned the Nazis from a fringe party into Germany's largest party by 1932
It made Germany rich enough to rearm
It ended the Treaty of Versailles
It caused Britain to support the Nazis
test.why: With roughly a third of the workforce jobless, voters turned to a party promising order and greatness, and Hindenburg appointed Hitler in 1933.

test.q: What do the Nazi and Stalinist states have in common that makes historians call both totalitarian?
choices: Both were monarchies
Both held free elections
Both tried to control every part of life and used terror against their own people
Both were created by the League of Nations
test.why: Their ideas were opposites, but their methods, total control backed by secret police, camps and propaganda, were much the same.

test.q: What pattern do the events from Manchuria in 1931 to Munich in 1938 show?
choices: Aggressors were stopped quickly by the League
Each time an aggressor got away with a seizure, the next demand was larger
The democracies attacked first
The Soviet Union defended every victim
test.why: Japan, Italy and Germany each took territory without being stopped, and appeasement at Munich was followed within months by the seizure of Czechoslovakia.

test.q: What kinds of evidence establish what happened in the Holocaust?
choices: Only rumors passed among soldiers
The Nazis' own records, Allied photographs and films of the camps, and survivor testimony
Novels written after the war
Guesses made by historians in the 1980s
test.why: Train schedules, camp registers and killing-squad reports, together with liberation footage and testimony at Nuremberg and since, document the planned murder of about six million Jews.

test.q: Why was the conflict between the superpowers after 1947 called a Cold War?
choices: It was fought only in winter
Neither side had nuclear weapons
It was fought entirely at sea
The United States and the Soviet Union competed for decades but never fought each other directly
test.why: The rivalry was fought with money, weapons, propaganda and other people's wars, such as Korea and Vietnam, rather than by direct battle.

test.q: What lesson did Kennedy and Khrushchev take from the Cuban Missile Crisis of 1962?
choices: That an enemy in a nuclear world needs a way out, which led to the hotline and a test ban treaty
That Cuba should be invaded
That air strikes always work
That treaties are useless
test.why: Each leader chose an exit that let the other save face, and both sides then began talking to make the rivalry less dangerous.

test.q: What did the American war in Vietnam and the Soviet war in Afghanistan have in common?
choices: Both ended with a superpower victory
Both were fought against France
A superpower with overwhelming firepower could not defeat local guerrillas and withdrew after heavy losses
Both lasted less than two years
test.why: In each war a superpower backed a weak government against guerrillas armed by its rival, and firepower could win battles but not the war.

test.q: What did Gandhi's Salt March of 1930 demonstrate?
choices: That India needed a larger army
That breaking an unjust law openly and accepting punishment without violence could shake an empire
That Britain would never leave India
That partition was the only answer
test.why: Gandhi's satyagraha turned a small act, picking up salt, into a challenge the empire could not answer without looking unjust before the world.

test.q: Which problem did most new African states inherit from colonial rule?
choices: Too many trained doctors and administrators
Membership in the Warsaw Pact
A lack of any natural resources
Borders drawn in Europe that cut across peoples, and economies built to export one or two raw materials
test.why: The flags changed in the 1950s and 1960s, but the borders of the 1880s and export economies priced abroad remained, as the Congo's collapse showed.

test.q: Why does the year 1948 carry two opposite names, the War of Independence and the Nakba?
choices: Because Israel and Egypt signed a peace treaty that year
Because the same events gave Jews a state after the Holocaust and drove about seven hundred thousand Palestinian Arabs from their homes
Because the United Nations refused to divide Palestine
Because the oil embargo began that year
test.why: Both memories describe real events: a state founded three years after the death camps and a people who locked their doors and never returned.

test.q: What single change made the peaceful revolutions of 1989 in Eastern Europe possible?
choices: Gorbachev's decision that the Soviet army would no longer save those governments from their own people
A NATO invasion
China's support for reform
A United Nations resolution
test.why: Without the threat of Soviet tanks, governments that had ruled by fear faced crowds in Leipzig, Prague and Berlin alone, and most would not order a massacre.

test.q: Which statement about globalization since 1991 does the unit support?
choices: Every person and place gained equally
No one gained at all
Only rich countries gained
The world as a whole grew richer and less poor while losses fell hard on particular places, such as factory towns in Illinois
test.why: Extreme poverty fell from about one in three people to under one in ten, while towns like Galesburg lost their largest employers and never fully recovered.

title: The Twentieth-Century World

chapters.title: The World Wars
chapters.bigQuestion: How did two world wars in thirty years change what governments could do to people, and what people expected from governments?

story.title: The Night the Guns Went Quiet
story.kicker: On Christmas Eve 1914, along a muddy line in Belgium, enemies who had been shooting at each other for months climbed out of their holes and shook hands.
paragraphs: The war was supposed to be over by Christmas. That is what the young men on both sides had been told in August 1914 when they marched off with flowers in their rifle barrels. By December the fighting had frozen into two lines of ditches that ran from the Swiss border to the North Sea. The men lived in them. Rain filled the trenches with cold water. Rats ate the food. Between the two lines lay a strip of mud, wire and unburied bodies that soldiers called no man's land.

On the evening of December 24, in several places along the line near the Belgian town of Ypres, British soldiers heard something strange from the German trenches. Singing. Some German units had put up small Christmas trees with candles on the edge of their trenches. The British answered with carols of their own. A few brave men shouted across the gap. Then a few climbed out, hands raised, and walked into no man's land. No one shot them.

By Christmas morning, in some sectors, hundreds of soldiers were standing in the open. They traded cigarettes, chocolate, buttons and newspapers. They showed each other photographs of wives and children. They helped bury the dead who had lain between the lines for weeks and held joint burial services. Letters home from both sides describe kicking a ball around, though the famous football match may have been several small kickabouts rather than one game. We know this happened because so many soldiers wrote about it, and British newspapers printed their letters in January 1915.

The generals were furious. Orders came down forbidding any contact with the enemy. Within days the shooting started again, and it would not stop for almost four more years. There was no repeat of the truce at Christmas 1915. By then too many men had died, and the bitterness ran too deep. Historians still argue about what the truce means. Some see proof that ordinary people did not want the war their governments had made. Others point out that the same men went back to killing each other within a week.

The truce is a good place to start the story of the twentieth century, because it holds both halves of that story at once. The century brought machines and governments powerful enough to kill millions. It also brought people who kept insisting, in trenches and prison camps and at negotiating tables, that there had to be another way. This chapter follows both.
story.think: The soldiers who traded cigarettes on Christmas Day were shooting at each other again a week later. What does that tell you about how much control ordinary soldiers had over the war?

lessons.title: Why Europe Went to War
lessons.mainIdea: World War I began when a single assassination pulled a web of alliances, rivalries and war plans into a conflict that no single government fully chose.
reading: On June 28, 1914, a nineteen-year-old Bosnian Serb named Gavrilo Princip stepped up to an open car in Sarajevo and shot Archduke Franz Ferdinand, the heir to the throne of Austria-Hungary. The Archduke and his wife died within minutes. Princip belonged to a group that wanted Bosnia freed from Austrian rule and joined to Serbia. Austria-Hungary blamed the Serbian government and, a month later, declared war on Serbia. Five weeks after a killing in a Balkan town, most of Europe was at war.

How did one murder do that? The answer is the *alliance* system. Over the previous forty years the great powers had signed promises to defend one another. Germany backed Austria-Hungary. Russia backed Serbia and was tied to France. France was tied to Britain. When Austria moved against Serbia, Russia began to gather its army. Germany, fearing a war on two fronts, declared war on Russia and then on France. Its war plan called for knocking out France fast by marching through neutral Belgium. When German troops crossed the Belgian border, Britain declared war on Germany. That was August 4, 1914.

Alliances explain the speed, but not the willingness. For decades the powers had been competing. Germany and Britain raced to build bigger battleships. France wanted back the provinces it had lost to Germany in 1871. Russia and Austria-Hungary both wanted influence in the Balkans as the Ottoman Empire weakened. Each country had taken colonies in Africa and Asia and feared the others would take more. This mix of *militarism*, which means treating military strength as the highest goal, and *nationalism*, an intense loyalty to one's own nation, made leaders confident that a short war would settle things in their favor.

Historians still argue over who was most to blame. Some point to Germany's decision to back Austria without limit. Some point to Russia's early mobilization, or to Austria's harsh demands on Serbia, or to the generals in every capital whose plans left no time for talking. What the evidence shows clearly is that nobody in July 1914 was planning a four-year war that would kill about nine million soldiers. They expected the war they remembered, quick and decisive. They got something no one had seen before.

words.d: a formal promise between countries to help each other, especially in war
the belief that a country should build up its armed forces and be ready to use them
intense pride in and loyalty to one's own nation, often at the expense of others
calling up an army and moving it toward the border to prepare for war

look.title: The Chain of Declarations
look.text: June 28: the Archduke is shot in Sarajevo. July 28: Austria-Hungary declares war on Serbia. July 30: Russia orders full mobilization. August 1: Germany declares war on Russia. August 3: Germany declares war on France. August 4: German troops enter Belgium; Britain declares war on Germany.
look.prompt: At which step in this chain could one leader have stopped the whole thing by choosing differently? What would that leader have risked?

check.q: Why did Britain declare war on Germany on August 4, 1914?
choices: German troops had marched into neutral Belgium
Germany had attacked British ships in the North Sea
Germany had declared war on Britain first
Britain wanted Germany's colonies in Africa
check.why: Germany's war plan sent its army through Belgium to reach France quickly, and Britain went to war when Belgium's neutrality was violated.

check.q: How did the alliance system turn a Balkan crisis into a European war?
choices: Alliances forced every country to stay neutral until attacked
Each country's promise to defend a partner pulled the next country in
The alliances had expired, so no one could stop the fighting
Serbia was a member of every alliance at once
check.why: Germany backed Austria, Russia backed Serbia, and France and Britain were tied to Russia, so each move triggered the next partner's entry.

check.q: What did leaders in July 1914 expect the war to be like?
choices: A four-year struggle that would kill millions
A war fought mainly at sea
A short, decisive war like the ones they remembered
A war with no clear winner
check.why: The reading says leaders expected a quick, decisive war and had no plan for the long struggle that followed.

lessons.title: Life and Death in the Trenches
lessons.mainIdea: New weapons made attacking almost suicidal, so the Western Front froze into trenches where millions died to move the line a few miles.
reading: The machine gun changed everything. A single gun crew could fire hundreds of bullets a minute, and a line of them could stop a charging regiment in its tracks. Artillery, the big guns, could now hit targets miles away. Barbed wire slowed attackers while the guns found them. Against all this, the soldier of 1914 still had a rifle, a bayonet and his legs. Both sides quickly learned that the only way to survive was to dig. By the end of 1914 the Western Front was a double line of *trenches*, deep ditches roofed with sandbags and timber, stretching more than four hundred miles across France and Belgium.

Life in the trenches was misery even when no one was attacking. Water pooled at the bottom, and men who stood in it for days got trench foot, a rotting of the skin that could cost a man his toes. Lice lived in every seam of every uniform. Rats grew fat on the dead. Shells could fall at any moment, and a hit could bury a whole dugout. Soldiers spent days in the front line, then rotated back to rest, then returned. Many wrote that the waiting was worse than the fighting.

When generals did order an attack, the results were terrible. The usual plan was to pound the enemy trench with artillery for days, then send infantry walking across *no man's land*, the strip of ground between the lines. The shelling rarely cut all the wire or killed all the machine gunners. On July 1, 1916, the first day of the Battle of the Somme, the British army suffered about fifty-seven thousand casualties, nearly twenty thousand of them dead, and gained almost nothing. The battle continued until November. At Verdun that same year, French and German armies fought for ten months over a few square miles and lost hundreds of thousands of men between them.

New weapons kept arriving: poison gas in 1915, tanks in 1916, aircraft that grew from scouts into bombers. None broke the deadlock for long. What finally moved the front in 1918 was exhaustion on one side. Germany launched huge spring attacks, gained ground, and then ran out of men and food. Fresh American troops, more than a million of them by the summer, tipped the balance. On November 11, 1918, at eleven in the morning, the guns stopped. Soldiers on both sides could hardly believe the silence.

the open ground between two enemy trench lines, covered by wire and gunfire
a soldier killed, wounded, captured or missing; the word counts all of them together
large guns that fire heavy shells over long distances

look.title: Military Deaths in World War I
look.cite: Standard estimates, rounded; exact counts differ by source

check.q: Why did both armies dig trenches instead of advancing in 1914?
choices: The soldiers refused to fight in the open
Generals wanted to save money on ammunition
Winter snow made marching impossible
Machine guns and artillery made charging across open ground deadly
check.why: The reading explains that machine guns, artillery and barbed wire stopped attackers, so digging in was the only way to survive.

check.q: What usually went wrong with a planned attack across no man's land?
choices: The artillery barrage warned the enemy but did not destroy the wire or the machine guns
Soldiers got lost because there were no maps
Attacks were only allowed at night
The tanks always broke down before reaching the wire
check.why: Days of shelling rarely cut all the wire or killed the gunners, so the walking infantry was cut down, as at the Somme in 1916.

check.q: Based on the reading, what finally ended the deadlock in 1918?
choices: A new weapon that broke through every trench
German exhaustion combined with fresh American troops
The arrival of poison gas
A peace treaty signed by the generals
check.why: Germany's spring attacks used up its men and food, while more than a million American soldiers added weight to the Allied side.

lessons.title: The War at Home
lessons.mainIdea: Total war pulled whole societies into the fight: factories, farms, women's labor, food rationing and government control of what people could say.
reading: World War I was the first *total war*, a war in which a country's entire economy and population are organized for fighting. Armies needed millions of shells a month, and only whole nations working together could make them. Governments took control of railroads, mines and factories. They told farmers what to grow and fixed the prices of bread and coal. In Germany, where a British naval blockade cut off imported food, the winter of 1916 to 1917 became known as the turnip winter because turnips were about all there was to eat. Hundreds of thousands of German civilians died of hunger and related disease during the war.

With so many men at the front, women filled the jobs they left. In Britain, France, Germany and later the United States, women made shells in munitions factories, drove streetcars, ran farms and worked as nurses close to the fighting. Munitions work was dangerous: the chemicals turned skin yellow, and explosions killed workers. Governments that had refused to let women vote now depended on their labor. In Britain, women over thirty won the vote in 1918. The United States passed the Nineteenth Amendment in 1920. The war did not cause these changes alone, but it made the old arguments against them hard to sustain.

Governments also went to war for people's minds. Every side produced *propaganda*, posters and films and news stories designed to make people hate the enemy and support the war. Britain and France spread stories of German atrocities in Belgium, some true and some invented. Germany did the same in reverse. Governments censored letters from the front so families would not learn how bad things were. In the United States, which entered the war in April 1917, a new law made it a crime to speak against the draft, and about two thousand people were prosecuted for what they said or wrote.

Total war reached across oceans. Britain and France brought hundreds of thousands of soldiers and laborers from India, Africa, Vietnam and the Caribbean. The United States sent more than two million men to France, and about three hundred and seventy thousand Black Americans served, mostly in labor units, though some fought with distinction beside French troops. In Illinois, factories in Chicago, Rockford and East St. Louis ran around the clock. The war set patterns that would return, larger, in the next one.

words.d: a war in which a nation's whole economy and population are organized to support the fighting
information, often one-sided or false, spread to shape what people believe
a government system that limits how much food or fuel each person may buy
using warships to stop supplies from reaching an enemy's ports

look.title: A President Explains a War Law
look.text: The Espionage Act of 1917 made it a crime, in wartime, to interfere with the armed forces or to obstruct military recruiting. In 1919 the Supreme Court upheld a conviction under it, ruling that speech may be punished when it creates a clear and present danger of harms that the government has a right to prevent.
look.cite: Schenck v. United States, Supreme Court, 1919 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: The Court said wartime speech could be limited when it creates a clear and present danger. Who decides what counts as danger? What is the risk in that?

check.q: What made World War I a total war?
choices: It was fought on every continent
Every soldier was a volunteer
Whole economies and populations were organized to support the fighting
Both sides used the same weapons
check.why: Total war means governments took control of factories, food and labor so the entire nation supported the army.

check.q: What caused the turnip winter in Germany?
choices: A failed turnip harvest across Europe
German farmers refused to grow wheat
The government banned bread to save fuel
A British naval blockade cut off imported food
check.why: The British blockade kept food imports out of Germany, and by the winter of 1916 to 1917 turnips were about all that was left.

check.q: How did the war change the argument over women's right to vote?
choices: It made the old arguments hard to sustain when governments depended on women's labor
It ended the argument because women stopped asking
It had no effect; the vote came decades later
It caused governments to take away rights women already had

lessons.title: Russia's Two Revolutions
lessons.mainIdea: War and hunger toppled the Russian tsar in March 1917, and eight months later Lenin's Bolsheviks seized power and pulled Russia out of the war.
reading: By early 1917 Russia was breaking under the war. Its army had lost millions of men. Its railroads could not carry both soldiers and food. In Petrograd, the capital, women stood in line for bread in the freezing cold and found the shelves empty. On March 8, 1917, thousands of women marched to demand bread. Workers joined them. The *tsar*, Nicholas II, ordered soldiers to fire on the crowds, but the soldiers refused and joined the marchers instead. Within a week Nicholas gave up his throne. Three centuries of rule by his family were over.

A temporary government of moderate politicians took over and promised elections. It made one fatal choice: it kept Russia in the war. Soldiers kept dying and deserting. Peasants seized land from nobles without waiting for permission. In cities, councils of workers and soldiers called *soviets* began acting like governments of their own. Into this chaos came Vladimir Lenin, a revolutionary who had spent years in exile. Germany, hoping he would take Russia out of the war, sent him home by train in April. His slogan was simple: peace, land and bread.

Lenin led the *Bolsheviks*, a disciplined party that believed in *communism*: the idea that workers should own the factories and land together, with no private owners and, eventually, no classes at all. On the night of November 6 to 7, 1917, armed Bolshevik supporters seized the bridges, telegraph offices and the Winter Palace in Petrograd. There was little fighting. The temporary government simply collapsed. Lenin announced a new government, took Russia out of the war in March 1918 by giving Germany huge stretches of territory, and moved the capital to Moscow.

Then came a civil war, from 1918 to 1921, between the Bolshevik Reds and a loose alliance of Whites who ranged from monarchists to democrats. The Reds won, partly because the Whites could not agree on what they wanted. Millions died in the fighting and in the famine that followed. The Bolsheviks shut down other parties, created a secret police and shot the tsar and his family. In 1922 they named the country the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics. For the next seventy years, the existence of a communist great power would shape politics on every continent.

words.d: the emperor of Russia before 1917
a council of workers or soldiers that acted as a local government in Russia in 1917
Lenin's communist party, which seized power in Russia in November 1917
a system in which the community, not private owners, holds factories and land, with the goal of a classless society

look.title: Peace, Land and Bread
look.text: Imagine you are a Russian soldier in the summer of 1917. Your officers order another attack. Your family writes that there is no bread at home and that the neighbors are dividing up the landlord's fields. One party says: keep fighting for our allies. Another says: peace now, land now, bread now.
look.prompt: Why would Lenin's three words win support that long speeches about democracy could not? What was the temporary government's mistake?

check.q: What event set off the revolution that ended the tsar's rule in March 1917?
choices: A German attack on Petrograd
Women marching for bread, joined by workers and then soldiers
Lenin's return from exile
The tsar's decision to leave the war
check.why: The bread march in Petrograd grew when workers joined and soldiers refused to fire, and within a week Nicholas II abdicated.

check.q: What was the temporary government's fatal choice?
choices: Moving the capital to Moscow
Giving land to the peasants too quickly
Keeping Russia in the war
Holding elections too early
check.why: Staying in the war kept soldiers dying and deserting, which gave Lenin's promise of peace its power.

check.q: Why did the Reds win the civil war, according to the reading?
choices: Germany sent troops to help them
The Reds promised to restore the tsar
The Whites had no weapons
The Whites could not agree on what they wanted
check.why: The Whites ranged from monarchists to democrats and could not unite, while the Bolsheviks were disciplined.

lessons.title: The Treaty That Settled Nothing
lessons.mainIdea: The Treaty of Versailles punished Germany, redrew the map of Europe and created a League of Nations, but left grievances that helped bring the next war.
reading: In January 1919 the victors met at Paris to write the peace. President Woodrow Wilson of the United States arrived as a hero. A year earlier he had laid out Fourteen Points for a fair peace: open diplomacy, freedom of the seas, the right of peoples to choose their own governments, and a League of Nations where countries would settle disputes by talking. The French leader, Georges Clemenceau, had other ideas. Germany had invaded France twice in fifty years. He wanted Germany weakened so it could never do so again. Britain's David Lloyd George stood between them.

The treaty signed at Versailles on June 28, 1919, five years to the day after Sarajevo, was mostly Clemenceau's. Germany lost about a tenth of its land and all its overseas colonies. Its army was limited to one hundred thousand men, with no air force, no submarines and no troops in the Rhineland along the French border. Article 231 made Germany accept responsibility for the war. On that basis Germany had to pay *reparations*, payments for the damage, set in 1921 at a sum so large that economists argued it could never be paid. Germans of every political view called it a dictated peace.

Other treaties broke up the losing empires. Austria-Hungary vanished, replaced by Austria, Hungary, Czechoslovakia and parts of Poland and Yugoslavia. The Ottoman Empire lost its Arab lands, which Britain and France took under a system called mandates. Wilson's idea of *self-determination*, that each people should rule itself, guided some of the new borders. But every new country contained minorities who had wanted to be somewhere else, and the principle was not applied to Asians or Africans at all. Delegates from Vietnam, Egypt and India who came to Paris asking for it were turned away.

The *League of Nations* was created, but without the country whose president had invented it. The United States Senate refused to approve the treaty, mainly over fears that the League could drag America into future wars. Germany and Russia were kept out at first. The League had no army. When strong countries broke the rules in the 1930s, it could only protest. The peace of 1919 has been blamed for too much and too little. It was harsh enough to enrage Germany and too weak to hold Germany down. That combination proved dangerous.

words.d: payments a defeated country is made to give the winners for war damage
the principle that a people should be able to choose its own government
an organization of countries formed in 1920 to prevent war through discussion and joint action
a former Ottoman or German territory that the League assigned to Britain or France to govern

look.title: Wilson's Aims
look.text: The program of the world's peace, therefore, is our program; and that program, the only possible program, as we see it, is this: I. lessons.title: A Depression Around the World
lessons.mainIdea: The crash of 1929 spread through debts, trade and banks until a quarter of workers in some countries had no job, and desperate people looked for anyone with answers.
reading: In October 1929 prices on the New York stock market collapsed. People who had borrowed money to buy shares could not pay it back. Banks that had lent to them failed, taking savings with them. Businesses that could not borrow cut production and fired workers. Workers with no wages stopped buying. By 1933 about one in four American workers had no job. In Chicago, families camped in shacks along the river, and the city could not pay its teachers for months. The *Great Depression* was the worst economic collapse the industrial world had seen.

It did not stay in America. During the 1920s American banks had lent heavily to Germany, and Germany had used the money to pay reparations to Britain and France, who used it to pay war debts to the United States. When American lending stopped, the whole circle broke. German banks failed in 1931. By 1932 about six million Germans, roughly a third of the workforce, were unemployed. Countries tried to protect their own workers by raising *tariffs*, taxes on imported goods. The United States raised them sharply in 1930. Other countries answered in kind, and world trade fell by more than half between 1929 and 1933.

The suffering was everywhere but unequal. In Britain the old coal and shipbuilding towns emptied out. In Japan, farmers who depended on selling silk to America watched the price collapse. In Latin America, countries that sold coffee, copper or beef to the world lost their buyers overnight. Peasants in colonies from India to Indonesia saw the prices of their crops fall while their taxes did not. Governments that had promised prosperity now seemed helpless. People asked whether *capitalism*, an economy run by private owners and free markets, could work at all.

Different countries gave different answers. In the United States, Franklin Roosevelt's New Deal put the government to work hiring the jobless, insuring bank deposits and paying pensions, all within a democracy. Sweden built a similar welfare system. The Soviet Union, cut off from world markets, reported no unemployment at all and drew admirers who did not see the costs. In Germany, Italy and Japan, the Depression helped bring to power men who promised order, jobs and greatness through force. The next lesson looks at them.

words.d: the worldwide economic collapse that began in 1929 and lasted through the 1930s
a tax on goods imported from another country
an economic system in which private owners run businesses and compete in markets
the condition of wanting a job and not being able to find one

lessons.title: Dictators of the 1930s
lessons.mainIdea: Mussolini, Hitler and Stalin built states that claimed total control over their people, using terror, propaganda and the promise of national greatness.
reading: The first of the new dictators was Benito Mussolini in Italy. Italy had been on the winning side in 1918 but felt cheated by the peace, and strikes and street fighting shook the country. Mussolini, a former socialist turned nationalist, organized squads of black-shirted veterans who beat up his opponents. In 1922 he marched on Rome, and the king made him prime minister. Within a few years he had banned other parties and jailed critics. He called his movement *fascism*: the nation and its leader above everything, violence as a virtue, democracy as weakness. The word comes from the fasces, a bundle of rods that symbolized authority in ancient Rome.

Adolf Hitler admired Mussolini and copied him. His Nazi party blamed Germany's defeat and misery on Jews, communists and the politicians who had signed the Versailles treaty. Through the prosperous late 1920s the Nazis were a fringe party. The Depression changed that. In the election of 1932 they became the largest party. On January 30, 1933, President Hindenburg made Hitler chancellor, believing he could be controlled. Within months Hitler had used a fire at the parliament building as an excuse to suspend civil rights, passed a law letting him rule by decree, banned other parties and opened the first concentration camp at Dachau. By 1934 he was the Führer, the leader, with no limits on his power.

Nazism was fascism with race at its center. Hitler taught that Germans were a master race and that Jews were a poison to be removed. The Nuremberg Laws of 1935 stripped German Jews of citizenship and banned marriage between Jews and other Germans. Jewish doctors, lawyers and teachers lost their jobs. On the night of November 9, 1938, Nazi mobs burned synagogues, smashed Jewish shops and sent about thirty thousand Jewish men to camps. Newspapers, radio, schools and youth groups all taught the same message. A state that tries to control every part of life this way is called *totalitarian*.

Joseph Stalin ruled the Soviet Union in the name of the opposite idea, communism, but his methods were much the same. From 1928 he forced peasants to give up their land to state-run collective farms. Those who resisted were shot or shipped to labor camps. The disruption caused a famine in 1932 and 1933, worst in Ukraine, that killed millions. Between 1936 and 1938 Stalin's secret police arrested hundreds of thousands of party members, officers, and ordinary people on invented charges; many were shot after staged trials. Fascist and communist states hated each other, but each showed what a modern government could do to its own people when nothing was allowed to stand in its way.

words.d: a political system that puts the nation and a single leader above all, glorifies violence and rejects democracy
describing a state that tries to control every part of public and private life
a ruler with total power who is not limited by law, elections or courts
a large state-run farm in the Soviet Union made by forcing peasants to give up their own land

lessons.title: The Road to War
lessons.mainIdea: Through the 1930s Japan, Italy and Germany seized territory step by step while the democracies, hoping to avoid another war, gave way until they could not.
reading: The first move came in Asia. In 1931 Japan's army seized Manchuria, a resource-rich region of northern China, and set up a puppet state. The League of Nations condemned the seizure. Japan simply walked out of the League. In 1937 Japan launched a full invasion of China. When its army took the capital, Nanjing, in December, soldiers murdered tens of thousands of prisoners and civilians and raped thousands of women over several weeks. Reports reached the outside world through diplomats, missionaries and journalists. The world protested and did nothing.

Mussolini watched and learned. In 1935 Italy invaded Ethiopia, one of only two independent countries left in Africa. Ethiopia's emperor, Haile Selassie, went to the League in person to ask for help. The League voted for mild trade penalties that did not include oil, and Italy completed its conquest. Then Hitler began. In 1936 he marched troops into the Rhineland, which the Versailles treaty had forbidden. France and Britain protested and did nothing. In March 1938 he took over Austria. Crowds in Vienna cheered.

The crisis came over Czechoslovakia, where about three million Germans lived in a border region called the Sudetenland. Hitler demanded it. In September 1938, at Munich, the British prime minister Neville Chamberlain and the French premier agreed to give it to him in exchange for a promise that Germany wanted nothing more. Czechoslovakia was not invited. This policy of giving a hostile power what it demands to avoid war is called *appeasement*. Chamberlain came home saying he had secured peace. Six months later Hitler took the rest of Czechoslovakia.

Why did the democracies give way so long? The memory of 1914 to 1918 was the biggest reason: no one wanted another Somme. Many believed Versailles had been unfair and that Hitler only wanted to correct it. Britain and France were not ready to fight, and the United States had passed laws to keep out of any European war. The Soviet Union, distrusted by all, made its own deal. On August 23, 1939, Hitler and Stalin signed a pact promising not to attack each other and secretly agreed to divide Poland. On September 1, Germany invaded Poland. Two days later Britain and France declared war.

words.d: giving a hostile power what it demands in the hope of avoiding war
a country that appears independent but is really controlled by another power
to take over a territory and make it part of your own country

lessons.title: A War on Every Ocean
lessons.mainIdea: World War II was fought across Europe, Asia, Africa and the Pacific; the turning points came at Stalingrad and Midway, and it ended with the total defeat of Germany and Japan.
reading: Germany's new way of war was called *blitzkrieg*, lightning war: tanks, trucks and dive-bombers punching through a front and racing ahead before the enemy could react. Poland fell in five weeks. In the spring of 1940 the same method took Denmark, Norway, the Netherlands, Belgium and, in six weeks, France. Britain stood alone under a new prime minister, Winston Churchill. Through the summer and fall of 1940, German bombers tried to destroy the British air force and then British cities. They failed. Britain survived, and its survival kept a base from which the war could later be carried back to Europe.

In June 1941 Hitler broke his pact and invaded the Soviet Union with more than three million men, the largest invasion in history. German armies reached the edge of Moscow by December. Then winter and Soviet resistance stopped them. The decisive battle came at Stalingrad on the Volga River, where from the fall of 1942 into February 1943 the two armies fought street by street until the Germans were surrounded and about ninety thousand survivors surrendered. From then on the Red Army pushed west. The Soviet Union lost more people in the war than any other country, roughly twenty-seven million by the standard estimate, most of them civilians.

The Pacific war began on December 7, 1941, when Japanese planes struck the American fleet at Pearl Harbor, Hawaii, killing about twenty-four hundred Americans. The United States declared war on Japan the next day, and Germany declared war on the United States. Japan quickly took the Philippines, Malaya, Singapore, Burma and the Dutch East Indies. In June 1942, at the Battle of Midway, American carriers sank four Japanese carriers in a single day and the tide turned. American forces then fought island by island toward Japan, at Guadalcanal, Saipan, Iwo Jima and Okinawa, each bloodier than the last.

On June 6, 1944, D-Day, American, British and Canadian troops landed on the beaches of Normandy in France and opened a second front in the west. Germany was now squeezed between the Red Army and the Western Allies. Hitler killed himself in Berlin on April 30, 1945, and Germany surrendered on May 8. The war had involved more than fifty countries and killed somewhere between fifty and eighty million people, most of them civilians, through fighting, bombing, starvation and murder. Japan fought on through the summer of 1945. The last lessons of this chapter explain how its war ended.

the countries fighting Germany, Italy and Japan, led by Britain, the Soviet Union and the United States
a new area of fighting that forces an enemy to split its army, as in Normandy in 1944
a warship that launches and lands aircraft, the key weapon of the Pacific war

lessons.title: The Holocaust
lessons.mainIdea: Nazi Germany and its helpers murdered about six million Jews and millions of others in a planned, industrial killing that we know about through the killers' own records and the survivors' testimony.
reading: The Nazis had persecuted Jews since 1933, but the war turned persecution into murder. When Germany conquered Poland in 1939, more than three million Polish Jews came under its control. They were forced into walled *ghettos* in cities like Warsaw, where hunger and disease killed thousands each month. When Germany invaded the Soviet Union in 1941, special killing squads followed the army, rounding up Jewish men, women and children, marching them to pits and shooting them. At Babi Yar, outside Kyiv, they killed more than thirty thousand people in two days in September 1941. By the end of the war these squads had shot well over a million people.

In January 1942 senior Nazi officials met at a villa in Wannsee, near Berlin, to organize what they called the final solution of the Jewish question: the murder of every Jew in Europe. The method was the death camp. At Auschwitz, Treblinka, Sobibor and other camps in occupied Poland, trains arrived from across Europe. Guards sorted the arrivals. Most were sent straight to gas chambers disguised as showers and killed with poison gas within hours. Their bodies were burned. A minority were worked to death. About one million Jews were killed at Auschwitz alone.

The Nazis also murdered Roma people, disabled people, Polish leaders, Soviet prisoners of war, gay men, political prisoners and Jehovah's Witnesses. The total of Jews murdered in the *Holocaust* is about six million, roughly two out of every three Jews in Europe. The killing required thousands of ordinary participants: railway clerks, police, factory managers, neighbors who pointed out hiding places. It also had resisters. Jews rose in the Warsaw ghetto in 1943 and fought for nearly a month. Denmark's people ferried almost all of the country's Jews to safety in Sweden. Individuals across Europe hid families at the risk of their own lives.

How do we know? The Nazis kept records: train schedules, camp registers, reports from the killing squads listing the numbers shot. Allied armies photographed and filmed the camps they liberated in 1945. Survivors testified at the Nuremberg trials, where the top Nazi leaders were tried, and have kept testifying since. The word *genocide*, the deliberate destruction of a people, was coined in 1944 to name what had happened, and in 1948 the new United Nations made it a crime. The Illinois Holocaust Museum in Skokie, founded by survivors who settled near Chicago, is one of many places where that evidence is kept.

words.d: the Nazi murder of about six million Jews and millions of others between 1941 and 1945
a walled section of a city where Jews were forced to live under Nazi rule
the deliberate destruction of a national, ethnic, racial or religious group
a camp built for the purpose of killing people in large numbers

lessons.title: The Bomb
lessons.mainIdea: Scientists working in secret, including at the University of Chicago, built a weapon that destroyed two cities in August 1945 and changed what war could mean.
reading: In 1939 physicists learned that splitting the nucleus of a uranium atom released enormous energy, and that a chain of such splits might make a bomb. Albert Einstein signed a letter warning President Roosevelt that Germany might build one first. The United States began a secret program, the *Manhattan Project*, that eventually employed more than a hundred thousand people. Its first great test happened in Illinois. On December 2, 1942, under the stands of an old football field at the University of Chicago, the physicist Enrico Fermi and his team started the world's first controlled nuclear *chain reaction*. It lasted a few minutes. It proved the bomb was possible.

The first bomb was tested in the New Mexico desert on July 16, 1945. By then Germany had surrendered, and the question was Japan. Japan's cities were already burning under American firebombing; one raid on Tokyo in March had killed around one hundred thousand people in a night. American planners expected an invasion of Japan to cost huge numbers of American and Japanese lives. President Harry Truman, who had taken office when Roosevelt died in April, decided to use the new weapon. On August 6 a single bomb destroyed the city of Hiroshima. On August 9 a second destroyed Nagasaki. Between them the bombs killed more than one hundred thousand people by the end of 1945, most of them civilians, and many more later from radiation.

On August 8 the Soviet Union declared war on Japan and poured into Manchuria. On August 15 Japan's emperor announced surrender in a radio broadcast. Most Japanese had never heard his voice. The war was over. Historians still argue about the decision. Some hold that the bombs ended the war quickly and saved lives on both sides. Others argue that Japan was already close to surrender, that the Soviet entry mattered as much as the bombs, or that a demonstration should have been tried first. The evidence supports parts of several views, which is why the debate continues.

What no one disputes is what the bomb meant for the future. A single aircraft could now erase a city. The Soviet Union tested its own bomb in 1949, and within a decade both sides had weapons hundreds of times more powerful than the one dropped on Hiroshima. Scientists who had built the bomb became some of the loudest voices for controlling it. The Chicago team's research grew into Argonne National Laboratory in the western suburbs, and the clock that Chicago scientists created to warn of nuclear danger, the Doomsday Clock, is still updated every year.

a process in which splitting one atom releases particles that split more atoms, releasing energy
invisible energy released by nuclear reactions that damages living cells

lessons.title: A New Order
lessons.mainIdea: The victors of 1945 built the United Nations to prevent another world war, but power now rested with two superpowers that were already drifting apart.
reading: In the spring of 1945, while the fighting still raged, delegates from fifty countries met in San Francisco to write the charter of a new organization. The *United Nations* was meant to fix what the League of Nations had gotten wrong. Every member would sit in a General Assembly. But real power went to a Security Council whose five permanent members, the United States, the Soviet Union, Britain, France and China, could each block any action with a *veto*. The founders accepted this because the great powers would not join otherwise. The United States Senate approved the charter by a huge majority. This time America was in.

The United Nations did more than debate. It set up agencies to feed refugees, fight disease and help children, and in 1948 it adopted a Universal Declaration of Human Rights listing the rights every person should have. It also created a court to try disputes between nations. Yet the veto meant the Security Council could act only when the great powers agreed, and within two years they rarely did. The UN could not stop wars between superpowers. It could sometimes limit or end wars where the superpowers were willing to let it.

The war had also rearranged the world's power. Britain and France were exhausted and deep in debt, and their empires in Asia and Africa would soon come apart. Germany and Japan lay in ruins under occupation. Two countries stood above the rest. The United States had lost about four hundred thousand soldiers but its cities were untouched, its factories were the world's largest, and it alone held the atomic bomb. The Soviet Union had suffered terribly, but the Red Army now occupied every capital from Berlin to Sofia. These two *superpowers* had fought Hitler together. They agreed on little else.

By 1947 the alliance was over. Stalin installed obedient governments across Eastern Europe. The United States pledged to help any country resisting communist takeover. Germany, and Berlin inside it, was split into zones. The next chapter follows the long, strange conflict that resulted, called the Cold War because the two sides never fought each other directly. But it began here, in the ruins of a war that had killed tens of millions and ended with a weapon that could kill everyone. The question of the second half of the century was whether the world had learned enough to avoid a third.

the power of one of the five permanent Security Council members to block any UN action
a country whose military and economic strength far exceed all others, as the United States and Soviet Union after 1945

story.title: The Note That Opened a Wall
story.kicker: On the evening of November 9, 1989, an East German official read a piece of paper he had not studied, and by midnight the most famous wall in the world was open.
paragraphs: For twenty-eight years the Berlin Wall had cut a city in half. It went up in August 1961 to stop East Germans from escaping to the West, and it worked: a concrete barrier, a strip of raked sand, guard towers, dogs, and orders to shoot. At least one hundred and forty people died trying to cross it. Families waved to each other across it on holidays. Children grew up never having seen the other side of their own street.

By the fall of 1989, East Germany was in trouble. Hungary had opened its border with Austria, and tens of thousands of East Germans were driving to Hungary and simply walking out. Every Monday, crowds in the city of Leipzig marched through the streets chanting that they were the people. The government, terrified of a bloodbath and without the backing of the Soviet leader, Mikhail Gorbachev, decided to ease travel rules to calm things down. A new regulation was drafted allowing citizens to apply for permits to travel abroad. It was supposed to take effect the next day, with paperwork.

That evening a party spokesman named Günter Schabowski held a televised press conference. Near the end, a reporter asked about travel. Schabowski, who had been handed the note just before the broadcast and had not read it carefully, fumbled through it and announced that East Germans could now cross the border. A reporter asked when. Schabowski looked at the paper, shrugged, and said: as far as I know, immediately, without delay. Television carried it live. Within an hour, West German news was reporting that the wall was open.

Thousands of East Berliners walked to the crossing points and demanded to be let through. The border guards had no orders. They phoned their superiors, who had no orders either. The crowds grew. Around eleven-thirty at night, the commander at the Bornholmer Street crossing, facing a crowd of thousands and fearing a stampede, opened the gate. Other crossings followed. East and West Berliners met on top of the wall, hugging strangers and hammering at the concrete with whatever they had.

No one had planned this. Not the East German government, not Gorbachev, not the Western leaders who watched on television with their mouths open. A system built on fear had run out of people willing to shoot. Within a year Germany was reunited. Within two years the Soviet Union itself was gone. This chapter tells the story of how the world came to be divided by that wall, what happened in the rest of the world while it stood, and why it fell.
story.think: The wall fell because guards without orders chose not to shoot. What had to change, over years, for that moment to be possible?

lessons.title: The Iron Curtain Falls
lessons.mainIdea: Between 1945 and 1949 the wartime alliance broke into two hostile blocs, one led by the United States and one by the Soviet Union, divided by what Churchill called an iron curtain.
reading: In February 1945, with Germany nearly beaten, Roosevelt, Churchill and Stalin met at Yalta on the Black Sea. They agreed to divide Germany into occupation zones and promised free elections in the countries the Red Army had liberated. Stalin had a different idea of free. Within two years, communist parties backed by Soviet troops and secret police had taken over Poland, Hungary, Romania and Bulgaria. Opposition leaders were jailed or killed. In March 1946 Winston Churchill, speaking in Fulton, Missouri, said that an *iron curtain* had come down across Europe from the Baltic Sea to the Adriatic. The phrase stuck.

Each side saw the other as the aggressor. To Americans, Stalin was swallowing Eastern Europe and would take the rest if he could. To Stalin, whose country had been invaded from the west twice in thirty years and had lost twenty-seven million people, a ring of friendly governments was simple self-defense, and the American bomb was the real threat. In 1947, when Britain could no longer afford to support the Greek government against communist rebels, President Truman asked Congress for money and announced that the United States would help any free people resisting takeover. This *containment* policy, holding communism where it was, guided American action for forty years.

The first great test came in Berlin. The city lay deep inside the Soviet zone of Germany but was itself divided into four sectors. In June 1948, angry that the Western powers were creating a separate West German state, Stalin cut every road and rail line into West Berlin. Two million people faced starvation. Rather than fight through, the United States and Britain flew in food and coal, a plane landing every few minutes for nearly a year. In May 1949 Stalin gave up and reopened the roads. The airlift had shown that the West would hold its ground without firing a shot.

By 1949 the division was fixed. Germany became two countries. In August the Soviet Union tested its own atomic bomb, years earlier than American experts had expected. In October communists won the civil war in China, the world's most populous country. Americans who had felt safe now felt surrounded. The *Cold War* was not a war in the old sense. The two sides never fought each other directly. It was a rivalry fought with money, spies, weapons, propaganda, and other people's wars, and for four decades it shaped almost everything that happened on the planet.

words.d: Churchill's phrase for the line dividing Soviet-controlled Eastern Europe from the West
the American policy of stopping communism from spreading beyond where it already held power
the rivalry between the United States and the Soviet Union from about 1947 to 1991, fought without direct war
a group of countries tied together under a leading power

lessons.title: Marshall Plan, NATO and the Warsaw Pact
lessons.mainIdea: The United States rebuilt Western Europe with money and bound it with a military alliance, and the Soviet Union answered with its own bloc.
reading: Two years after the war, Western Europe was still broken. Cities lay in rubble, factories had no fuel, and the winter of 1947 was one of the coldest on record. Hungry, jobless people were voting for communist parties in France and Italy. In June 1947 the American Secretary of State, George Marshall, proposed that the United States pay to rebuild Europe. Over four years the *Marshall Plan* sent about thirteen billion dollars, a huge sum then, in food, machinery and raw materials to sixteen countries. The Soviet Union refused to take part and forbade its satellites to join. Western Europe's economy recovered faster than anyone had predicted.

The plan was generous and it was also strategy. Americans reasoned that prosperous people would not vote for communism, and that a rebuilt Europe would buy American goods. Both things happened. Then the Berlin blockade convinced Western leaders that they needed more than money. In April 1949 the United States, Canada and ten Western European countries signed the North Atlantic Treaty. Its key clause said that an attack on any member would be treated as an attack on all. This alliance, *NATO*, was the first peacetime military alliance the United States had ever joined. It broke with a tradition of avoiding foreign entanglements that went back to George Washington.

The Soviet Union built a mirror image. Its economic answer to the Marshall Plan tied the economies of Eastern Europe to Moscow. When West Germany joined NATO in 1955, the Soviet Union and its seven satellites signed the *Warsaw Pact*, a military alliance under Soviet command. On paper it was an alliance of equals. In practice, Soviet troops stayed in each member country, and when Hungarians rose against their government in 1956 and Czechoslovaks tried to reform theirs in 1968, Warsaw Pact tanks crushed them. NATO protested and did nothing, because doing something risked nuclear war.

Europe thus settled into two armed camps that faced each other across a line running through the middle of Germany. Behind that line, the two blocs built two different ways of life. Western Europe combined capitalism with welfare states, elections and open borders among its members. Eastern Europe had state-owned economies, one-party rule, and borders that its own citizens could not cross. The gap in wealth between the two halves grew every year, and people on the eastern side could see it on Western television. That gap, more than any army, eventually decided the contest.

words.d: the American program from 1948 to 1952 that gave about thirteen billion dollars to rebuild Western Europe
the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, a military alliance of the United States, Canada and Western Europe formed in 1949
the military alliance of the Soviet Union and its Eastern European satellites, formed in 1955
a country that is formally independent but controlled by a stronger neighbor

lessons.title: Living with the Bomb
lessons.mainIdea: Both superpowers built enough nuclear weapons to destroy each other many times over, and the fear of that outcome kept them talking even as they competed.
reading: In 1952 the United States tested a hydrogen bomb hundreds of times more powerful than the one that destroyed Hiroshima. The Soviet Union tested its own the next year. In October 1957 the Soviets launched Sputnik, the first satellite, which meant a rocket could now carry a bomb across an ocean in half an hour. Americans were shaken. Both sides built missiles by the thousands, in underground silos, on bombers, and on submarines hidden under the sea. By the 1980s the two arsenals together held tens of thousands of warheads, enough to destroy every large city on Earth.

Strategists gave this situation a name that was also a description: *mutual assured destruction*, or MAD. If either side attacked, the other would still have enough weapons left to destroy the attacker. So neither side could win, and neither dared start. Some argued that the bomb had therefore prevented a third world war. Others pointed out that it had come frighteningly close to failing. Schoolchildren in Chicago and every other American city practiced hiding under their desks. Families built fallout shelters in their basements. The threat of the bomb was part of daily life.

The Cuban Missile Crisis of October 1962, covered in the next section, scared both sides enough to begin talking. A telephone hotline linked Washington and Moscow. In 1963 they agreed to stop testing bombs in the air. In the early 1970s President Richard Nixon and the Soviet leader Leonid Brezhnev signed the first treaty limiting missile numbers, and Nixon traveled to both Moscow and, in 1972, to communist China, which had split with the Soviet Union. This easing of tension was called *détente*, a French word for relaxing. It did not end the rivalry, but it made the rivalry more predictable.

Détente faded in the late 1970s and the arms race sped up again. Then in the mid-1980s a new Soviet leader, Mikhail Gorbachev, and President Ronald Reagan, who had called the Soviet Union an evil empire, surprised the world by becoming partners. In 1987 they signed a treaty that for the first time eliminated an entire class of nuclear missiles rather than just limiting them. Verification teams from each country inspected the other's bases. The bomb had not gone away. But the two men who controlled most of them had decided that having fewer was safer than having more.

words.d: a competition between countries to build more and better weapons than each other
the idea that a nuclear attack by either side would lead to the destruction of both, so neither dares strike
a period of eased tension between the superpowers in the 1970s, marked by treaties and visits
the explosive part of a missile or bomb

sections.title: Hot Wars in a Cold War

lessons.title: China's Revolution and the Korean War
lessons.mainIdea: Communist victory in China in 1949 and the invasion of South Korea in 1950 turned the Cold War into shooting wars in Asia.
reading: China had been at war with itself, on and off, since the 1920s. On one side stood the Nationalists under Chiang Kai-shek, backed by the United States. On the other stood the communists under Mao Zedong, who built their strength among peasants in the countryside. The Japanese invasion of 1937 nearly destroyed the Nationalist armies, while the communists grew by fighting behind Japanese lines. When the civil war resumed after 1945, Mao's forces won. On October 1, 1949, he proclaimed the People's Republic of China in Beijing. Chiang fled to the island of Taiwan, which the United States protected. Two Chinas claimed to be the real one.

Mao's new state took land from landlords and gave it to peasants, then took it back into collective farms. In 1958 he launched the Great Leap Forward, ordering villages to make steel in backyard furnaces and report impossible harvests. The result was the deadliest famine of the century, with estimated deaths in the tens of millions between 1959 and 1961. In 1966 Mao unleashed the Cultural Revolution, sending bands of young Red Guards to attack teachers, officials and anyone accused of old thinking. Schools closed for years. Mao died in 1976, and his successors quietly began to undo much of what he had built.

Korea had been split at the end of World War II along the thirty-eighth parallel, Soviet troops in the north and American in the south. On June 25, 1950, North Korean forces crossed the line. Within weeks they held almost the whole peninsula. Because the Soviet delegate was boycotting the UN Security Council that month, the United States got the UN to authorize a force under General Douglas MacArthur. A daring landing at Inchon in September cut the North Korean army in half, and UN troops pushed north almost to the Chinese border. Then, in November, hundreds of thousands of Chinese soldiers poured across it.

The war seesawed back to the middle and then froze there. Fighting dragged on until an *armistice*, a stop to the fighting without a peace treaty, was signed in July 1953. The line ended up almost where it had begun. About thirty-six thousand Americans died, and Korean deaths, soldiers and civilians together, ran into the millions. Korea is still divided. The war showed the pattern of the whole Cold War: the superpowers never fought each other directly, but the countries in between paid the price. Korea also convinced Americans to keep a large army forever and to see every communist gain, anywhere, as a Soviet move.

the Chinese party led by Chiang Kai-shek that lost the civil war and retreated to Taiwan
a line of latitude on a map; Korea was divided at the thirty-eighth

lessons.title: Thirteen Days over Cuba
lessons.mainIdea: In October 1962 the discovery of Soviet missiles in Cuba brought the superpowers closer to nuclear war than at any other moment, and both leaders chose to step back.
reading: Cuba lies about ninety miles from Florida. In 1959 a young lawyer named Fidel Castro led a rebel army that overthrew a corrupt dictator friendly to the United States. Castro took over American-owned sugar mills and oil refineries, and when Washington cut off trade, he turned to the Soviet Union. In April 1961 the United States armed and landed about fourteen hundred Cuban exiles at the Bay of Pigs to overthrow him. The invasion failed within three days. Castro declared himself a communist, and the Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev saw a chance to plant weapons at America's door.

In the summer of 1962 Soviet ships secretly carried nuclear missiles to Cuba. On October 14 an American spy plane photographed the launch sites under construction. President John F. Kennedy and his advisers debated for a week in secret. The generals urged air strikes and invasion. Kennedy feared that would kill Soviet troops and start a war in Europe. On October 22 he went on television, showed the world the photographs, and announced a naval *quarantine*: American warships would stop any vessel carrying weapons to Cuba. Soviet ships kept coming. The world waited to see whether they would stop.

For the next six days nothing was certain. Soviet ships turned back from the quarantine line. But work on the missile sites continued, an American spy plane was shot down over Cuba, and American forces went to their highest alert short of war. Khrushchev sent two letters, one emotional and offering to remove the missiles if the United States promised not to invade Cuba, and a second, harder, demanding that America also remove its missiles from Turkey. Kennedy answered the first letter publicly and, through his brother Robert, secretly promised to remove the Turkish missiles later. On October 28 Khrushchev announced the missiles would go.

Decades later, records showed how close it had been. Soviet commanders in Cuba had short-range nuclear weapons and might have used them against an invasion. A Soviet submarine officer, out of contact and believing war had begun, refused to agree to fire a nuclear torpedo. Both leaders had been pushed by their own advisers to be tougher, and both had chosen a way out that let the other save face. The crisis led directly to the hotline and the test ban treaty. It also taught both sides a lesson they never forgot: in a nuclear world, an enemy needs an exit.

a person forced to live outside his or her own country
pushing a dangerous situation to the edge of war to force the other side to back down

choices: The United States cut off trade after he seized American-owned businesses

check.why: After Castro took American sugar mills and refineries and Washington ended trade, he looked for a new partner and protector.

check.why: Kennedy wanted pressure without a first shot that could trigger war in Europe, and the quarantine left room for an exit.

check.why: The public deal was a no-invasion promise; the secret part was the later removal of the Turkish missiles, which let both sides save face.

lessons.title: Vietnam and Afghanistan
lessons.mainIdea: Each superpower fought a long war against a determined local enemy, in Vietnam and in Afghanistan, and each lost, at great cost to the people whose country it was.
reading: Vietnam had been a French colony since the 1800s. On September 2, 1945, days after Japan's surrender, a nationalist and communist named Ho Chi Minh declared Vietnam independent in Hanoi, opening his speech with words borrowed from the American Declaration of Independence. France refused to let go. After eight years of war, French forces were surrounded and defeated at Dien Bien Phu in 1954. A conference at Geneva split Vietnam temporarily at the seventeenth parallel, with Ho's communists in the north and a government friendly to the West in the south, and promised elections to reunite it. The elections were never held. The United States feared Ho would win them.

American leaders believed in the *domino theory*: if Vietnam fell to communism, its neighbors would fall one after another. So they backed South Vietnam with money, advisers, and after 1965 with soldiers, more than half a million by 1969. The enemy was the North Vietnamese army and southern guerrillas called the Viet Cong, who fought from the villages and jungle, struck and vanished. American forces had the firepower to win any battle and no way to win the war. Bombing, chemical defoliants and the burning of villages turned many Vietnamese against the Americans and turned many Americans against the war. In January 1968 the communists launched the Tet Offensive, attacking cities across the south; they were beaten back, but television showed Americans a war their leaders had said was nearly won.

Protests grew, especially on college campuses. In 1968 Chicago's Democratic convention was surrounded by demonstrators and police clashes filled the news. President Nixon slowly withdrew American troops while widening the bombing, and in January 1973 signed an agreement that got the last of them out. Two years later, in April 1975, North Vietnamese tanks rolled into Saigon and the war ended with a united communist Vietnam. About fifty-eight thousand Americans had died. Vietnamese deaths, north and south, soldiers and civilians, are estimated at well over a million. The dominoes did not fall beyond Vietnam's immediate neighbors.

The Soviet Union then made a mirror-image mistake. In December 1979 it sent its army into Afghanistan to prop up a failing communist government. Afghan fighters called *mujahideen*, armed by the United States, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia, fought a guerrilla war from the mountains. Soviet firepower could take any valley and hold none. After nine years and about fifteen thousand Soviet dead, along with perhaps a million Afghans, Gorbachev withdrew the last troops in February 1989. The war drained Soviet money and morale at the moment its empire was cracking. Afghanistan itself fell into civil war, with consequences that reached the United States in 2001.

a fighter who is not part of a regular army and uses surprise attacks and hiding among civilians
the Afghan fighters who resisted the Soviet occupation from 1979 to 1989
the surprise communist attacks across South Vietnam in January 1968 that shook American confidence

lessons.title: Gandhi and the Partition of India
lessons.mainIdea: Gandhi's movement of nonviolent resistance helped end British rule in India in 1947, but independence came with a partition that killed hundreds of thousands.
reading: In 1930 a thin man of sixty in a homespun cloth walked from his home in western India toward the sea, about two hundred and forty miles, with a growing crowd behind him. When Mohandas Gandhi reached the beach at Dandi, he picked up a lump of salt. Under British law only the government could make salt, and every Indian paid a tax on it. Gandhi's act was a crime, and he meant it to be. Across India tens of thousands followed his example, and the British jailed about sixty thousand people. The Salt March showed the world a new kind of weapon, and it showed Indians that the empire could be defied.

Gandhi called his method *satyagraha*, which he translated as truth force. It meant refusing to obey unjust laws, accepting arrest and beating without striking back, and treating even the oppressor as a person who could change. It required more discipline than fighting. Gandhi trained in South Africa, where he had spent twenty years defending Indian workers against discrimination. He also believed that India must be one nation of Hindus, Muslims, Sikhs and everyone else. Many Indians disagreed with his tactics, and the Muslim League, led by Muhammad Ali Jinnah, came to demand a separate Muslim state.

World War II broke Britain's grip. Britain had used India's soldiers and money without asking, and Indian leaders were jailed for demanding independence in return. After the war Britain was bankrupt, and a new government decided to leave. The question was whether to leave one country or two. As violence between Hindus and Muslims spread in 1946 and 1947, Britain agreed to *partition*: India for the Hindu majority, Pakistan, in two pieces a thousand miles apart, for Muslims. Independence came at midnight on August 14 to 15, 1947. Gandhi refused to celebrate. He spent the day fasting for peace.

Partition set off one of the largest migrations in history. Something like fifteen million people crossed the new borders in both directions, Muslims to Pakistan and Hindus and Sikhs to India. Trains arrived full of the dead. Estimates of the killed run from several hundred thousand to over a million. In January 1948 a Hindu extremist who thought Gandhi too generous to Muslims shot him dead in Delhi. India and Pakistan have fought several wars since. Yet India became, and has remained, the world's largest democracy, and Gandhi's method traveled: Martin Luther King Jr. studied it, and civil rights marchers in Chicago and Selma used it.

words.d: Gandhi's method of nonviolent resistance, which he called truth force
dividing a country into separate states, as India and Pakistan in 1947
deliberately breaking an unjust law in public and accepting the punishment
a territory ruled by a distant country for that country's benefit

lessons.title: Africa Wins Independence
lessons.mainIdea: Between 1957 and the mid-1970s almost every colony in Africa became independent, some by negotiation and some by war, but colonial borders and economies remained.
reading: At midnight on March 6, 1957, a crowd gathered in the capital of the British colony of the Gold Coast. The British flag came down. The flag of a new nation, Ghana, went up. Its first leader, Kwame Nkrumah, had studied in the United States. He had organized strikes and boycotts. The British had jailed him, then released him to govern. Ghana was the first colony in sub-Saharan Africa to win independence. Nkrumah told the crowd that its freedom meant nothing unless it was linked to the freedom of the whole continent. Across Africa, people listened.

The colonial powers had been weakened by World War II, and African soldiers who had fought in it came home asking why they should be ruled by strangers. The Cold War also helped: both superpowers, for their own reasons, said they opposed old-style empires. In 1960 alone, seventeen African countries became independent, most of them former French colonies. Britain let its colonies go over the next decade, usually after negotiations. Belgium abandoned the huge Congo in 1960 with almost no preparation, having trained only a handful of Congolese as doctors, officers or administrators, and the country fell into chaos within days.

Where many European settlers lived, independence came through war. In Algeria, more than a million French settlers wanted to stay French. The war from 1954 to 1962 killed hundreds of thousands of Algerians and involved torture and terror on both sides before France finally withdrew. In Kenya, Britain fought a rebellion in the 1950s and held tens of thousands of Kikuyu people in camps. Portugal clung to Angola and Mozambique until 1975. In each case, independence came, but the memory of the fighting shaped the new states.

Independence did not undo the colonial past. The new borders had been drawn in Europe in the 1880s and cut across peoples and languages, leaving nearly every state with groups that distrusted one another. Colonial economies had been built to export one or two raw materials, cocoa or copper or oil, and the price of those was set abroad. Many new leaders, including Nkrumah, became dictators, and armies overthrew governments in country after country. The superpowers backed rival sides in civil wars in Angola, Ethiopia and elsewhere. Africans had won the right to govern themselves. Whether they could build the states they wanted was a struggle that continued.
